contributions.headingText: Chondroblastoma is a benign tumour of bone that has a predilection for epiphyseal or apophyseal regions, composed of chondroblastic cells and islands of eosinophilic chondroid matrix.
2E82.Z & XH4NK2 Benign chondrogenic tumours, site unspecified & Chondroblastoma NOS

Approximately 75% of chondroblastomas involve the epiphyseal (subchondral) region of long bones, with the femur being the most commonly affected site, followed by the proximal tibia and proximal humerus {2793161; 4023729}. Other sites include the talus, calcaneus, patella, and pelvic bones (especially the acetabulum). Less frequently, the ribs, vertebrae, and small bones of the hands and feet are affected. Involvement of craniofacial bones is exceptional. In adult patients aged > 30 years, short tubular bones and flat bones, rather than long bones, are more commonly affected {5051664; 2793161}.

Signs and symptoms

The clinical presentation varies with the site of disease. The most common symptom is pain. Local tenderness, joint effusion, impaired movement, and muscle atrophy may be found as presenting symptoms.

Imaging

Radiographically, a well-defined, often sclerotically marginated lucent lesion is present, showing geographical bone destruction. Chondroblastoma is typically located adjacent to a growth plate, usually in the epiphysis or in the epiphysis and metaphysis, and rarely in the metaphysis or apophysis only {4712761; 4023729; 5051664}. The lesions are usually < 5 cm {2793161}. Mineralization, trabeculation, cortical erosion, and expansion are frequently present; expansion is more common in flat and small bones {4023729}. MRI characteristically exhibits reactive changes outside the tumour, which are reflected by synovitis and periosteal reaction also distant from the tumour, as well as increased signal intensity in bone and surrounding soft tissues on fluid-sensitive and gadolinium chelate–enhanced images {4023729; 5051664; 2793161}. The tumour itself is inhomogeneous and has areas of low signal intensity on fluid-sensitive sequences due to mineralization and trabeculation, which are also well seen on CT {6470260}. Aneurysmal bone cyst–like changes can be seen as fluid-fluid levels on MRI in areas of marked expansion {19936740; 10524855}.

Chondroblastomas account for < 1% of all bone tumours. Most occur in patients with an immature skeleton in the second to early third decades of life (10–25 years of age), although it may present at any age {4023729; 28634924; 2793161}. It is twice as prevalent in males {8253461; 4023729; 2793161}.

H3.3 alterations are seen in various tumour types including bone tumours like chondroblastoma and giant cell tumour of bone. Specific substitutions are associated with different tumour types: p.Lys36Met with chondroblastoma and p.Gly34Trp with giant cell tumours of bone, suggesting that specific substitutions provide a growth advantage to specific cell types {24162739; 30582658}. p.Lys36Met substitutions in chondroblastoma are more frequent in the H3-3B (H3F3B) gene on chromosome 17 {24162739; 27499898}.

The p.Lys36Met mutations inhibit the H3K36 methyltransferases NSD2 (MMSET) and SETD2, which results in reduced global H3K36 methylation {27229140; 27474439}. These epigenetic pathway alterations probably block mesenchymal differentiation and influence tumorigenesis in chondroblastoma {30098026; 25453099; 30101054}.

Macroscopically, chondroblastomas are usually well-defined eccentric lesions with a thin sclerotic rim. The features vary from soft to rubbery with gritty and haemorrhagic areas. Chondroid matrix may be prominent. Blood-filled spaces may be seen in some cases with aneurysmal bone cyst change {5051664; 5445403}.

Histologically, chondroblastomas are composed of sheets of ovoid to polygonal cells with small singular grooved nuclei and eosinophilic cytoplasm {14880556; 5051664}. The cytoplasmic border is usually distinct. Epithelioid cells may be present. There are interspersed osteoclast-like giant cells and islands of eosinophilic chondroid matrix. Basophilic hyaline cartilage is infrequent. Pericellular lace-like or chicken-wire calcification is characteristic and usually noted among degenerative cells. Nuclear atypia and/or mitotic figures may be found. Aneurysmal bone cyst–like change is common.

Immunohistochemistry

Immunohistochemistry using an antibody against H3.3B (H3F3B) p.Lys36Met (K36M) shows diffuse nuclear expression in > 96% of the cases and is helpful in small biopsies or cases with extensive aneurysmal bone cyst–like change {26844533; 26457357}. SOX9, S100, cytokeratin, and DOG1, although not specific, may be focally positive {19801163; 2579018; 1692005; 26402312}.

Differential diagnosis

The differential diagnosis includes primary aneurysmal bone cyst, giant cell tumour of bone, clear cell chondrosarcoma, chondromyxoid fibroma, Langerhans cell histiocytosis, and an extremely rare subtype of osteosarcoma: chondroblastoma-like osteosarcoma {10192265}.

The vast majority of chondroblastomas harbour a p.Lys36Met substitution in one of the genes that encode H3.3: H3-3B (H3F3B) (> 95%) on chromosome 17 or, less frequently, H3-3A (H3F3A) on chromosome 1 {24162739; 26844533; 26457357}. Among bone tumours, this is highly specific for chondroblastoma, although one case of clear cell chondrosarcoma was reported to harbour an H3-3B (H3F3B) p.Lys36Met mutation {24162739}. IDH1 and IDH2 substitutions are not seen in chondroblastomas {22074484; 21598255; 26457357}.

Essential: epiphyseal/apophyseal location; sheets of chondroblastic cells, island of eosinophilic chondroid matrix and osteoclast-like giant cells.

Desirable: a fine network of pericellular chicken-wire calcification; presence of H3.3 mutation demonstrated by p.Lys36Met (K36M) expression or H3-3A (H3F3A) / H3-3B (H3F3B) mutation analysis.

Chondroblastomas are benign tumours that in > 80% of the cases are successfully treated with surgical curettage with or without adjuvant treatment of the surgical bed {30418383; 15972914}. Radiofrequency ablation may be used {19304917}. The recurrence rates vary with site of disease, being lower in long bones and higher in flat bones and craniofacial bones, ranging from 10% to 18% {30418383; 15972914; 3604981; 8253461}. There are no reliable histological parameters predicting local recurrence {8253461; 12913842; 28971570}. In exceptional cases, so-called benign lung metastasis may develop {16007463}.
